t: except with a document that reaches her. With a written document that will be given to her.

and that the content of the document be that he divorced her and removed her from his acquisition. That the content of the document be that the husband sends the woman away and that she is not his acquisition, and not that he sent himself away from her (see below, halakhot 3-4).
and that its content be something that cuts between him and her. That the get be given in a way that completely severs the bond between them.
and that it be written for her sake. That the writing of the get be done for the sake of divorcing a particular woman (see below 3:3).
and that no further act be lacking after its writing except giving it to her. That there be no need for any additional act before giving it, such as cutting it from something attached (below 5:6).
and that he give it to her in the manner of divorce. And not for another purpose (below 3:9).
the date. Writing the date in the get.
by rabbinic law. By the Sages' enactment.
for he divorces only by his wish. There is no divorce unless the husband agrees to it (and see below 2:20).

but the woman is divorced with her wish and without her wish. The divorce is valid whether done with the woman's consent or not. 3. A thing that cuts... that no authority remain to him over her. The get separates them completely, with nothing remaining that places restrictions on her in any matter by force of the marriage to her husband.
as will be explained. Below 8:5-14.
that the get be given into her hand... as will be explained. Below 5:1.
for he is the one who sends her away. That the husband divorces the woman, as will be explained.
behold, you are sent away etc.. These expressions convey his wish to divorce her and remove her from his acquisition.
and the body of the get. The essence of the get (for the text of the get see below 4:12).
'behold, you are a free woman' is not a get. This is the wording for freeing slaves, and is not suitable for divorcing a woman (see Hilchot Avadim 5:3).
its point is not that her divorce is not complete until she leaves his house. For the divorce does not depend on this at all.
even though she is still in his house, as will be explained. Below 5:8.

but if he divorced and did not remove her from his house... she needs a second get from him. If they were secluded together before witnesses after the divorce, we worry that he cohabited with her for the sake of betrothal.
she needs a second get from him, as will be explained. Below 10:17-18.
for only writing and giving are lacking. That it can be given immediately after it is written.
this excludes something that lacks cutting. Something requiring detachment from its place of growth, which is a significant act.
on something attached. To the ground, for example if he wrote on a leaf attached to a tree.
the form (tofes). The fixed text of the document.

the name of the man and the name of the woman and the date and 'behold you are permitted to any man'. The main part of the get, called the 'toref' (below 3:17), in which the details that vary from get to get are written.

and they signed. On it the witnesses. Perhaps it should be vocalized 'vachatamo', that the husband had the witnesses sign the get. 8. A perforated pot. A clay vessel perforated at the bottom, whose growths are considered attached to the ground (Hilchot Terumot 5:15).

even though he gave her the whole pot... a decree lest he cut. Lest he cut the leaf after writing, and because the plant is considered attached they decreed regarding it even if he can give it without detaching it.

but he may write on a shard of a pot and give it to her. One may write on the vessel itself, which is considered detached even though what grows in it is considered attached (see Hilchot Mekhirah 3:15-16).
in the manner that it is a document of debt. That he told her he was giving her a document of debt.
that he put it in her hand while she was asleep. That she did not receive it knowingly.
and if he said to her afterwards. After giving it to her as another document or while she was asleep, and his final statement joins his giving (Rabbi David Ibn Zimra).
he said to the witnesses, 'See a get etc.'. Even without the woman's knowledge, since one can divorce her even without her consent (above halakhah 2).
kinsi. Receive.
who was embarrassed. Who was ashamed, but did not retract from defining the giving as for a get.

but if he had been speaking with her about the matter of her get. If they had previously spoken about their divorce matters, from the context it can be understood that giving the get was for divorce (for a similar law regarding betrothal see Hilchot Ishut 3:8).
but if he bowed his body toward her or extended his hand. By bowing his body toward her he brought the get tied to him close to her.
let the matter be established. Let the matter be upheld and given validity.

and it is impossible that this woman be forbidden today etc.. It cannot be that there is such a significant change in the woman's status without witnesses to the matter. For before her divorce she is a married woman, among the severe forbidden relations (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 1:6), and after the divorce she is permitted to any man.
when is this said. That the get has no validity at all.
if the husband wrote... this is an invalid get. By the Torah the husband's handwriting is considered testimony (Tosafot, Gittin 3b), but the Sages disqualified it (see below 2:7, 10:1-2).
and the get in her hand turns out to be like a shard of the earth's shards. The get is likened to a shard and worthless, since no one testifies to its truth.
by witnesses of delivery. Who testify to the delivery of the get to the woman.
between him and her. Without witnesses present.

that the witnesses of delivery were found disqualified. It became clear that at that time they were disqualified from testimony, such as transgressors or relatives (see Hilchot Edut 10:1-2, ibid. chapter 13).

since the witnesses in it are valid and the get comes out from under her hand. In this case there is no challenging the validity of the get, and if it is in her possession we are like witnesses that it was delivered to her (Yad Peshutah, based on the Ran).
disqualified ones testified from within it. The two disqualified witnesses signed the get.
for it is found as if forged from within. The disqualified witnesses signed on the get damage its credibility (see below 3:8).

he distanced the witnesses from the writing by the full space of two lines. There is a gap of two lines between the end of the get and the signature of the witnesses, which allows forgery of the document (see Hilchot Malveh Veloveh 27:4).
where the get came out from under her hand etc.. In such a case the get relies on the witnesses signed on it.
they must read it. In order to know that this is indeed her get.
and if he gave it to her in their presence at first, they go back etc.. Where he gave it without their having read it beforehand, they read it after the giving.
they read it while it was in the husband's hand etc.. Before it was handed to the woman.
they read it again. Lest he switched it for another document when it was put into his hand.
but she took it and threw it into the sea or the fire. The get was destroyed, and it can no longer be determined whether the husband switched the get when it was put into his hand.
and he gave her a get etc.. He told the witnesses that it was a get, but they did not verify it (R. Y. Kafah).
and they found a mezuzah or another document. They searched for the get among the barrels, but found only a mezuzah parchment or another document, and no get.
we do not worry about her. We do not worry about a divorce, and she is not divorced, since we must assume he intended to mislead her and threw her a mezuzah or a document instead of a get.

two or three mezuzot were found there etc.. In this case it is proven that mezuzot were lying among the barrels, and the previous assumption that he threw her a mezuzah is nullified, and it is possible that he threw her a get that was not found there.
provided that they recognize the language of the get. Provided that they understand what is written in it.
they trace for them etc.. They mark the letters of their names on the get with non-permanent writing, and the witnesses sign over the marking.
and one does not do so with other documents. In which witnesses who do not know how to write are not made to sign by signing over a tracing (Hilchot Malveh Veloveh 24:6).

it is a light matter, that they were lenient in women's gittin so that Jewish women should not be agunot. There is a special leniency in gittin to use such witnesses, so that women will not remain without permission to marry others, if gittin were scrutinized as strictly as other documents.
since the signing of the witnesses on a get is by their words. By the Sages' enactment, and they themselves were lenient in their enactment in certain cases.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 15.
they spell out their names in the get. They write their names explicitly.
for they sign only one in the presence of the other. One in the presence of the other (the reason for the enactment and the disqualification is explained below 9:29).
that he write the date in the get etc.. That in every get the date be written, as in other documents.

lest his wife be his relative and commit adultery etc.. If she is his relative, he might want to cover up that she committed adultery, and give her a get so she can claim that the get was given before the adultery, and she was not married at that time. They therefore enacted that the writing date be written in the get, to prevent this kind of deception.
earlier or later. The date written in it is earlier or later than the date on which the get was actually written, although a debt document dated later is valid (Hilchot Malveh Veloveh 23:1-2).
in the night following it. When the day had already changed.

even though they were engaged in the same matter. They were occupied with writing the get from the day into the night, in which case other documents are valid (ibid. halakhah 3). All the changes here disqualify the get because it turns out that false testimony is written in it (Commentary on the Mishnah, Gittin 2:2).
he cut off the date from it. He cut off from the get the part containing the date.
or did not write the name of the day. The exact date.
in the first or second week of such-and-such month. In the first or second week of a particular month.
in such-and-such shavua. A particular shemittah cycle (a unit of seven years) among the seven cycles of each jubilee.

valid. If he cut off the date it is valid, since this is noticeable and no one can be deceived by it. And if the date written in the get is not specific, it still has some value in that he could not cover up his relative's adultery up to that time.
this day on which the get was issued. The day on which it was handed to the woman.
by the reign of that time. According to the government at that time.
for the sake of the peace of the kingdom. For the government was particular about this.
of the Creation. Of the creation of the world.

by the reign of Alexander of Macedon, which is the count of documents. A count that was customary in the days of the Sages and the Geonim. It began in the year 3450 from the creation of the world, 311 BCE (see Hilchot Shemittah Veyovel 10:4). [Note: in some manuscripts the reading is 'Alexander Makron', and see R. Y. Kafah's note in his edition.]
and if he wrote by the reign of that time etc.. After they became accustomed to write by the Creation or by the count of documents.
authority. Government.
so that the get turns out to be void. For example, they erred in the names of the man and woman.
as will be explained. Below 2:8.
like other documents. For example in a debt document (Hilchot Malveh Veloveh 23:6).

and they are his agents and they are his witnesses. The agents themselves can also be the witnesses of the divorce, and there is no need for other witnesses since the agent becomes a witness (Hilchot Ishut 3:16). He divorces with it whenever he wishes. Even if they give it to her a long time after writing and signing. 3. Even though his wife is not with him. Because the woman's consent to the divorce is not needed (above 1:1).

that the witnesses and the scribe recognize and know that this is so-and-so and his wife is so-and-so. For in every document written in the presence of one party, there is concern that incorrect names might be written in it and the document used for fraud (Hilchot Malveh Veloveh 24:3). Some explained that the scribe must know their names so that the get be written for her sake (see below 3:1, R. Y. Kafah and Yad Peshutah).
in the presence of his fellow. In his presence.

lest... and bring it to his fellow's wife and divorce her with it. And then the fellow's wife could claim that her husband divorced her. 4. In time of danger they write etc. When there is no possibility of delaying until witnesses and a scribe who know the man and woman are found, they were lenient in the matter because of agunah.
and the woman pays the scribe's fee. For if the scribe's fee were imposed on the husband, he might avoid writing a get and leave his wife an agunah (Babylonian Talmud Bava Batra 168a).
and the husband must say on his own to the scribe etc.. That he appoints them explicitly to write and sign.
this is an invalid get. For one cannot appoint an agent to command another (see also Hilchot Zechiyah Umatanah 4:10).

and they deliberate on this matter at length because it is close to being a void get. The judges must examine this halakhah carefully, since the ruling in it is not decisive (R. Y. Kafah), or because the husband's intent must be well clarified (see Yad Peshutah).
and what is the difference between invalid and void etc.. Explained at length below 10:1-2.
these shall give it to her. Without worrying that the get may be invalid.
these write another. Because they became agents for the divorce, and their agency is not cancelled until she is divorced.
that they reconsider. That they consult him and receive permission from him anew.
for he did not make them for divorce. He did not ask them to complete the divorce.
send her away. As in the language of the verse: 'and sends her away from his house' (Deuteronomy 24:1).
shivkuha, tarkuha. Words that are part of the text of the get, whose only meaning is divorce: 'document of divorces... and letter of release' (below 4:12).
they shall write a valid get. For all these are expressions specific to divorce.
provide for her. Take care of her needs (Rashi, Gittin 65b).
as the law... as the custom. As the rule.
he has said nothing. Although these expressions might hint at divorce, their plain meaning is different.
and they do not give to his wife etc.. For he did not command them to give.
and one led out in a collar. He is taken out chained to a post for trial.
and one who sails at sea. One who sets sail in a ship.
and one who goes out with a caravan. On a distant journey.

for it is known etc.. That it is clear he wanted to divorce her, so that she not be an agunah if he does not return, or not need levirate marriage if he dies (and see Hilchot Berakhot 10:8), and when he said 'write' he also meant that they give.
and they wrote and gave it to her. Immediately, although he did not explicitly command to give it to her.
this is a valid get. Since it is reasonable that he intended to divorce her before he died, as above for one in danger.
he went up on the roof and the wind pushed him, it is not a get. For he died in an accident, and so he has the law of a healthy person who did not intend that the get be given to the woman.

if it is uncertain whether he threw himself or the wind pushed him, it is a get. In such a case, the proximity between the command to write the get and the death leads us to assume there is a connection between them, and that he meant to say that they should give the get.
provided that they know him. Provided that those who hear recognize that person.
and even if they lifted him up and did not recognize him, the get is valid. For his face may have changed after death (Yad Peshutah).
like a time of danger. As above, halakhah 4.
who suffered severe wounds etc.. Wounds that will certainly cause death.
the majority of both simanim was slaughtered in him. Most of the windpipe and the gullet were cut, so that there is no doubt he will die soon (below 13:17).
and he gestured etc.. For he cannot speak.
one whom an evil spirit terrifies. Afflicted by an attack of madness.
for his mind is not sound and settled. And at that moment he is like a deaf-mute or imbecile.
who reached the drunkenness of Lot. So drunk that he is not aware of his actions at all, like Lot, whose daughters lay with him without his knowing at all (Genesis 19:33-35).
he was terrified. He went mad.
we wait until he recovers. For at present he is like an imbecile with no mind, and cannot divorce.
one who became mute and his mind is sound. Who cannot speak but is of sound mind.
and he nodded with his head. He answered 'yes' with a movement of the head.
we examine him three times in alternation etc.. We ask him questions at intervals to test whether he can answer them properly.
his mind became deranged. He went mad.
for the law of one who became mute is not like the law of a deaf-mute. Explained in the next halakhah.
who marries. Who takes as a wife.
a pikei'ach. An ordinary person, neither deaf-mute nor imbecile (Hilchot Ishut 2:26).
gesturing of a deaf-mute. Instruction by movements of the hands and body.
as we have explained. Ibid. 4:9.

one who betroths a minor through her father etc.. The father receives betrothal on behalf of his daughter until she is twelve years and a day old and has signs of maturity in her body (Hilchot Ishut 2:1, 3:11), and the same applies to a get.
he divorced her when she was a na'arah etc.. She is a na'arah for six months after she grows two hairs (ibid. 2:1-2), and her father still has authority over her and receives her betrothal.
and a betrothed na'arah does not appoint an agent etc.. For she is not yet married and has not left her father's authority (ibid. 3:12).
if she can distinguish between her get and something else. If she is able to understand that a particular document is important and that she must keep it.
one whom the law requires to be compelled to divorce etc.. That by law he is obligated to divorce her.
they beat him until he says 'I want to'. For a man divorces only willingly (above 1:1), and they afflict him until he is willing to divorce her.
they compelled him. They forced him.

since the law requires him to write, it is an invalid get. By the Sages' enactment. But had the court's ruling not obligated him to write, the get would be void by the Torah, since it was done under compulsion.
and why is this get not void etc.. For although he said he wants to, it is clear that it was done against his true will.
but one whom his evil inclination overpowered... and was beaten until he did... he is not compelled. He is not considered compelled by us, who beat him.
rather he compelled himself by his evil mind. He forced himself to act contrary to halakhah.

since he wants to be of Israel etc.. His true will is to act according to halakhah. Therefore this beating is not within the category of compulsion, but on the contrary it removes the compulsion from the man and reveals his will.
laymen. Who are not expert in the laws.
it is an invalid get. Although it should be void (since it was given under compulsion and without justification), they decreed that it be invalid because it resembles a valid compelled get as above.
and if gentiles compelled him to divorce unlawfully, it is not a get. For it does not resemble a valid get at all.
a scribe. One whose profession is writing documents.
to teach or to learn. To teach others the text of the get, or to practice himself.
it is not a get even though it was written for the sake of divorce. Because it was not written for the sake of that particular couple.
and he reconsidered. He regretted.
and the scribe wrote with this intention. The scribe intended that the husband decide which of his wives to divorce with it.
even though he passed a quill over it for her sake. He wrote the words again over the written words, and in this retracing he intended it for her sake.
and he was secluded with her. They were alone together, and perhaps he cohabited with her.
she is divorced and may marry with it from the outset. The get is entirely valid, even to permit her to marry another.

a decree lest they say her get preceded her son. For he might give her the get a long time after it was written, and in the meantime a child may be born to her from him. People might think she was divorced from the date written in the get, and that the child was born of adultery.
it shall be with me. It shall be kept with me.
for she was not a woman of divorce from him. At the time it was written there was as yet no connection between them, and their divorce had no meaning.
write a get for my betrothed. He had already betrothed that woman, and she is thus subject to divorce.
and he married her. And took her as a wife.
valid. But it is an old get (as above, halakhah 5).
he wrote it for his yevamah etc.. She was his brother's wife, and the brother died without children. He wrote her a get before performing yibbum in order to divorce her with it after marrying her.
this is a doubtful divorce, since she is not a complete wife. There is a bond of marriage between them, but she is not considered fully his wife (see for example Hilchot Yibbum Vachalitzah 1:14).
a scribe who wrote forms of gittin. Who prepared in advance a document with the fixed text of a get.

and left the place of the man etc.. He left in them room for adding these details - the names and the essence of the get ('behold you are permitted') - which must be written for his sake and her sake.

it is invalid. Lest he also write in advance the details that must be written for her sake (the 'toref'). [Note: there is another version of this halakhah: 'Because of the scribe's livelihood the Sages permitted the scribe to write forms of gittin, leaving the place of the man, the place of the woman, the place of the date and the place of 'behold you are permitted to any man', so that he write them for the sake of the divorcing man and the divorced woman, and likewise the witnesses shall sign for his sake and her sake'. This is the first edition of the book, and afterward the Rambam retracted and corrected it as we have it (Yad Peshutah; and see below halakhot 17-18).]

for the witnesses sign on the get only for the repair of the world. Lest he give her a get before two and they die (above 1:15). And because the witnesses' signing is by the Sages' enactment, their signing not for her sake does not void the get (by the Torah) but makes it invalid (by the Sages).
since it is like forged from within. In the get itself there is something that impairs its validity, like the signature of disqualified witnesses (above 1:16).

but like forged, not definitely forged. Since being not for her sake is not visible in the document, there is no conclusive proof in the document that it is forged, and so it is not void but only invalid.
in a place where caravans are not frequent. A place that is not a thoroughfare for the public, so there is no concern that the get fell from passersby.
and she may be divorced with it. And she may be divorced with it, and we do not worry that it is another get with identical names that was not written for this divorce.
and no one had yet stayed there. Although people passed there, they had not yet had time to stay for any length (see the next halakhah).
recognition by eye (tevi'ut ayin). Identification by general familiarity, without a specific sign.
when it was rolled up. While it was coiled.
in its presumption. That it was not switched.
it is established in that place. It is known that in the husband's place there is a person with a name identical to his.
a distinctive sign. A clear sign by which it can be proven that it is the same get.
two who sent two gittin. And their names are identical.
and they got mixed up. The gittin, and it is not apparent which belongs to whom.
by witnesses of delivery. By witnesses testifying to the delivery of the get, as is the law of the Torah (above 1:13).
and every name that he has. To include other names that were not written.
he wrote his nickname and her nickname. His or her epithet.
who converted out of Judaism (nishtamed). Who changed his religion.
he is like a gentile for all matters. For many laws, since the commandments of Shabbat and idolatry are equal to the entire Torah (see Hilchot Shabbat 30:15).

and a gentile writes according to his own mind. Even if a Jew told him to intend it for her sake, he acts only according to his own mind, and will not write the get for her sake (for a similar halakhah see Hilchot Tefillin 1:11).
they are not of sound mind. And therefore cannot write for her sake.
he is not subject to gittin and betrothals. He cannot betroth or divorce (Hilchot Ishut 4:15), and therefore is invalid even for writing the get.
behold you are permitted to any man. For this is the essence of the get (above 1:4).
this is a valid get. After the fact they validated it, because by law only the toref must be written for her sake (Commentary on the Mishnah, Gittin 2:5, and see the next halakhah).
it is permitted to leave a deaf-mute, imbecile etc.. They forbade only that a scribe write forms, lest he write the toref, but in these they did not disqualify.
provided that an adult stands over them. A person of understanding supervises them so they do not write the toref (Commentary on the Mishnah, Gittin 2:5).
a gentile and a slave, one does not have them write the form from the outset. Because they act according to their own mind, and they might also write the toref (ibid.).

for they permitted writing forms of gittin only because of the scribe's livelihood. It seems this wording follows the first edition, which permitted writing forms because of the scribe's livelihood, and this is also the reason for permitting from the outset a form written by a deaf-mute, imbecile or minor (see above halakhah 7 in the explanation and in the poskim). In the corrected copy of the book that was in the yeshiva in Egypt a responsum attributed to the Rambam was cited in which he corrected here too, in accordance with the final edition above halakhah 7, and erased the word 'except' (Yad Peshutah).
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 7.

she is divorced. Even though the document was written with Shabbat desecration, it is valid, since it was inadvertent (and he does not have the law of one who publicly desecrates Shabbat mentioned above in halakhah 15).
and they gave it to her. Without valid witnesses of delivery.
for the witnesses are disqualified by the Torah. One who commits a transgression punishable by lashes is disqualified from testimony (Hilchot Edut 10:1-3).
he wrote it on a festival deliberately... it is invalid. By the Sages' enactment, since they wrote it in transgression, but it is not void by the Torah like a get written on Shabbat deliberately.
whose mark stands. The writing lasts a long time (see Hilchot Shabbat 11:15).
and sikra. Red dye.
and komos and kalkantos. Kinds of salts that dye in a blackish shade.
with lead (avar). Lead.
with shachor. Soot.
and with shichor. Charcoal.
and one does not write with them from the outset. Because the writing is not clear in brightness and sharpness (Yad Peshutah).

with gall-nut water. Water in which gall-nuts were soaked, whose color is yellow-brown (R. Y. Kafah). Gall-nuts are growths that develop on various plants (such as the terebinth and the boxthorn), and contain substances used in the leather-tanning industry and in making ink (compare Hilchot Tefillin 1:4).
a scroll of gall-nut. Parchment treated with gall-nuts.
because it is not recognizable. Because their color resembles the parchment.
things forbidden for benefit. Materials that it is forbidden to use and which therefore have no value, since there is no need for the document to have any value.
and one writes on something that can be forged etc.. A material on which the writing can be altered, leaving the witnesses' signature, without the forgery being noticeable.
erased paper. Paper whose writing was already erased, so that a further erasure is not noticeable on it.
the diftera. Hide whose processing was not completed, on which erasure is not noticeable.
and on the hand of a slave. Even though after a time the writing fades.
comes out from under her hand. The slave is in her possession.
for it cannot be forged. Since a tattoo is not erased.
and even if the slave was established as his. It was known that the slave belongs to the husband.
and she says 'it was delivered to me before witnesses'. There are witnesses of delivery, but no witnesses are signed on the slave's hand.
lest he came to her on his own. Arrived at her, and was not delivered to her by the husband as a get.

for walking things have no presumption. Slaves and animals that walk from place to place on their own, we do not assume that ownership of them belongs to the one in whose possession they are found, but proof is needed that they were given to him properly (see Hilchot To'en Venit'an 10:1-4). Compare the next halakhah.
the tablet. A board.
for the woman herself writes her get. She may write the get on something belonging to her and give it to the husband to divorce her with it.
for the validation of the get is only by its signers. The witnesses give validity to the get (above 1:16), and testify that it was done properly.
he engraved the get on the board etc.. He did not write the get, but engraved the letters deep into the board.
a sheet of metal. A thin beaten sheet.
he hollowed out the thighs of the letters. He engraved the body of the letters themselves.
'written with an iron pen', meaning he digs. From this verse it emerges that engraving with an iron pen is called 'writing'.

he engraved the thighs from behind the sheet until they protruded on the face of the sheet. He pressed the shape of the letters into the back of the sheet so that they protrude on its front side. He dug out the inside of the letter until the thighs appear raised on both sides. He beat out or scraped the background inside and around the letters until they stand out.
for this is not writing. No action was done to the body of the letters.
one who tattoos the form of writing on the skin. He engraves in it the shape of letters.
who marked on the skin the form of writing. He marked by scratching.
in any script. In any type of letters.
and in any language. In any language.
that they recognize the language of the writing and its script. That they understand the language in which the get is written and the letters in which it was written.
in the script of another language. In the form of letters of another language.
that they not have two meanings. That they cannot be understood in two ways.
the minors who recognize that script. Children who understand this script.
who are neither wise nor foolish... but average. Who are not very wise or very foolish, but average.
since it is read for the matter of divorce etc.. Since it can be understood as a divorce document, it is not void by the Torah but only invalid by the Sages.

the text of the get. On such-and-such day of the week, such-and-such day of such-and-such month, in such-and-such year from the creation of the world - or by the count of documents - by the count we are accustomed to count in such-and-such place. How I, so-and-so son of so-and-so, from such-and-such place, and any other name and epithet that I and my fathers and my place and the place of my fathers have, wished of my own will, without being compelled, and released and left and divorced you to yourself, you so-and-so daughter of so-and-so, from such-and-such city, and any other name and epithet that you and your fathers and your place and the place of your fathers have, who were my wife previously. And now I have released and left and divorced you to yourself, so that you may be permitted and in control of yourself to go and marry any man you wish, and no man shall object to you in my name, from this day forever, and behold you are permitted to any man. And this shall be for you from me a document of divorce and a get of release and a letter of leaving, according to the law of Moses and Israel.
as we have explained. Above 1:15.

'and if you are gat', meaning if you commit adultery. The Aramaic translation of the words 've'i garat' is 'if she committed adultery', implying that this document would take effect only if she commits adultery.
'li mehach', meaning I am laughing. For that is the Aramaic translation of 'mechach', so that the document was given in jest.
lest the reader read 'tihvayin'. 'You (f. pl.) shall be.' Therefore it is written with three yods.
and likewise he shall lengthen the vav of 'vechadu'. He shall lengthen the last vav in the word 'vechadu' (meaning 'and now').
of terukhin and shivkin. Divorces and release.
terikhin and shevikin. Divorced and released ones.
a word. A whole word.
that he hung between the lines. He initially omitted a letter or word, and afterward wrote them in the gap between the lines.
he went back and specified at the end of the get. He went back and wrote explicitly at the end of the get before the place of the witnesses' signature.
on an erasure. Written over writing that was erased.
valid. For there is no concern of forgery, as is done with other documents (see Hilchot Malveh Veloveh 27:8).
torn warp and weft. Torn lengthwise and crosswise, in the way the court tears documents so they will not be used again (see Hilchot Malveh Veloveh 23:14).
was eaten away. Was diminished.
like a sieve. Like a strainer.
and its image remains. The impression of the letters.
when is this said. That the gittin mentioned in the previous halakhot 15-16 are invalid.
when the get came out from under her hand with signing witnesses. That its validity is by virtue of the witnesses signed on it, like any document.
it is valid. Because witnesses of delivery are effective even when the document was not made properly (as above, halakhot 2-3).
if they wrote it as a whole. In a unified text that includes the divorcing couples.
if this scroll was given to each of them with witnesses of delivery, all of them are divorced. For each of them was given her get, though no witnesses are signed on it.
if it was the one whose get is last, that the witnesses are read with it. The scroll is with the owner of the bottom get, the one after which the witnesses are written immediately.

and if the scroll came out from under the hand of one of the first ones, she is doubtfully divorced. For it is possible that the witnesses' signature is only on the last get and not on those before it.

he wrote 'I so-and-so and so-and-so and so-and-so divorced our wives so-and-so and so-and-so'. From the text of this get it is not apparent that a particular husband divorces his wife, but all are included together.
in two columns in one scroll, side by side. In two columns on one sheet.
coming from beneath this one to beneath that one. That the signatures of the witnesses extend from the bottom of one column to the bottom of the other column.
for the witnesses are read with her get. The witnesses' signature appears to belong to that get.
he joined the top of this sheet to the top of that sheet, with the witnesses in the middle. He joined the tops of two gittin, and two witnesses signed between the tops.
he left part of the get and wrote it on the second column. He wrote part of the get in the second column of the sheet.

provided that it is evident on the scroll that it was not cut and that this is what the scribe intended. Provided it is evident that the end of the get in the second column did not belong to another get whose top was cut off, and that the scribe intended to complete the get in the second column.
he joined these words to the words of the get. The greeting is attached to the get by the connecting vav, and the witnesses' signature thus applies to both matters together.
the meaning of the verse is not that the get must reach her hand etc.. The meaning of what is stated in the Torah is not that the get must reach specifically her hand, but rather her domain.
or her agent, whom she made his hand like her hand. An agent whose authority she strengthened to receive the get in her place (see below 6:1).
it is all one. All are considered her domain.

and even though it is a courtyard in which the get will be kept. Even though it is a courtyard in which objects are guarded, which for acquisition acquires for its owner even in his absence (see Hilchot Zechiyah Umatanah 4:9), for a get it does not acquire until the woman stands beside it.

for divorce is a detriment to her etc.. The rule is that one confers benefit on a person in his absence, but one does not impose a detriment on him except in his presence (Hilchot Mekhirah 29:11; Hilchot Zechiyah Umatanah 4:2), meaning that one may grant a person a monetary or legal right in his absence, but not create something to his detriment. Therefore the courtyard does not acquire the get for the woman without her presence.
once it reached the airspace of the roof parapet's partitions. The get entered the space enclosed by the partitions of the roof's parapet. See the diagram on the previous page.
within three handbreadths of the roof. Where there are no partitions, the get reached close to the roof, and is considered as already lying on it.
provided that it is coming down to rest. That it will end up resting on the roof.
he threw into her domain into the fire... it is not a get. For it did not reach her domain. 6. He threw it on a reed.
or a spear stuck in her domain etc.. A pole or javelin stuck in the ground, where a get lying on its high end is not guarded in the airspace of partitions.
two courtyards, one inside the other etc.. The woman's courtyard surrounded by the husband's courtyard.
once he threw the get into the airspace of the outer one. He threw the get above the inner courtyard, at a place opposite the height of the outer partitions.
for the inner is guarded by the walls of the outer. The inner courtyard too is guarded by the height of the outer partitions.

which is not so with baskets. If these are baskets placed one inside the other, the law is not as with courtyards - the height of the outer basket's partitions does not help to guard the inner basket (as will be explained below).
even if it reached the airspace of the inner one. Inside it, but did not rest in it, for vessels do not acquire in the airspace of their partitions at all.

when it was tilted on its side and has no base. When the inner basket is tilted on its side and leans on the wall of the outer basket (Magid Ma'aseh), because the inner basket has no flat bottom but its lower part is pointed (Yad Peshutah, and see Hilchot Korban Pesach 1:13). In such a case, the inner basket's location is not fixed, and therefore the husband is not particular about it.
a flask. A bottle.
a kefifah. A basket.
it is a separate domain. It is considered another domain.
and the place of the bed's legs is not. For the bed's legs stand in his domain.
and he did not designate it. He did not fix where the place he lent her is.

and it reached her four cubits... she is divorced. For four cubits is a person's place (see Hilchot Shabbat 11:15; Hilchot Gezelah Va'avedah 17:8), and it became clear that this is the place he lent her.
it rolled and fell on a beam or a rock far from her. It did not land by her, but rolled outside her four cubits.
and it has no name 'levi'. There is no special name for that place that distinguishes it from the rest of the courtyard.

he has not set aside a domain for himself etc.. If it has no such distinguishing features, it is not considered another place, and it too is within the area that the husband lent the woman (Kesef Mishneh).
and he lent her one place etc.. That is the place where she stands, so the get did not reach her domain.
even though it passed within three handbreadths near the ground. Although by the law of lavud the get is considered as already on the ground (as above, halakhah 3).
unless it was going to rest in her domain. And in this case it fell outside her domain.
if she can extend her hand and take it. If it is possible for her to extend her hand from her roof to the roof where the get lies, and take it.

for although residences are divided above as they are divided below etc.. Although ownership of roofs is divided according to the division of the houses beneath them, so that this roof's place is not hers, nevertheless the owners are not particular about such a use, since she does not actually enter their roof.
a katafras. Sloping downward like a slope.
near to him... half and half. These terms will be explained in the next halakhah, and they do not concern distance alone but the ability to guard the get.
doubtfully divorced. See below 10:3.
it was near enough to her that she could bend and pick it up. That she can bend over and lift it.
it is invalid. See below 10:2.

it is invalid until the get reaches her hand. Although such closeness is like her domain (see Hilchot Ishut 4:22), the Sages were stringent regarding a domain that is not both of theirs, so that it must reach her actual hand.
she stood opposite him. The woman came and stood facing him, near the boundary of his four cubits.

if the get was within his four cubits she is not divorced, even though if she bends she can pick it up. Although the get is very near her, since those four cubits are like the husband's domain, as he stood there before she came.

even though it is half and half etc.. Unlike the law above (halakhah 13), where in half-and-half she is doubtfully divorced, here the get is invalid because she stood there first, and it is her four cubits.
until the get reaches her hand. For they were stringent in a domain that is not both of theirs (as above, halakhah 13).
tied with a cord. The get was tied to a string.
if he can detach it and bring it to him. That the husband can pull the get from her hand to himself by it.
until the cord is cut. Until the string is cut.

he put the get in the hand of her slave... and she guards it. Since the slave is her property, for the get to be acquired for her by his grasp as the acquisition of a courtyard, she must stand beside him (as explained above, halakhah 2).

even if bound, it is not a get. Even if the slave is tied and cannot walk, this is not a 'courtyard guarded with her knowledge', since it is guarded with the slave's knowledge. [Note: this text was also before the Tur and other early authorities. But before the Rashba, the Ran and the Maggid Mishneh there was a different reading in the Rambam: 'If he was bound, it is a get and as if it reached her courtyard, for she stands beside it; and if he was not bound, it is not a get'.]
asleep and she guards it, it is invalid. Because he is able to walk, and a walking courtyard does not acquire (Hilchot Mekhirah 3:12-13).
and if he was bound, she is divorced. For he does not walk at all.
and wrote her a deed of gift of him. The husband gave the woman the slave as a gift.
since the courtyard is acquired by document, money or possession. Which are the ways land is acquired (see Hilchot Mekhirah chapter 1).
the agent that the woman appoints... is called an agent of receipt. He is not an agent to carry the get, but was appointed to receive the get in the woman's place.

and she must appoint him before two witnesses. To appoint him before two witnesses, just as the divorce must be done before witnesses (see above 1:13), so too this agency, because by the agent's receiving the divorce the woman's status changes (see Yad Peshutah, and Hilchot Ishut 3:15).
and even if they are the first ones. The witnesses of the appointment can also serve as witnesses of delivery.
when is this said. That witnesses of delivery are also needed.
where the get was lost or torn. And there is no proof that the get was actually delivered to the agent.

its coming out from under his hand is like its coming out from under the woman's hands. Just as if the get is in her possession, witnesses of signing suffice (above 1:16), so is the law when the get is in his possession.
like the woman herself. Above 1:15-16.
the husband cannot appoint an agent to receive a get for his wife. He has no power to appoint a person to receive the get in her place.
and an agent of carrying and bringing does not need witnesses. At the time of appointment, since they serve in a practical agency and do not substantively replace the sender (as above, halakhah 1).
except... the non-Jew and the slave. Because the laws of betrothal and divorce do not apply to them (see Hilchot Ishut 3:17).
and the deaf-mute, the imbecile and the minor. Who lack understanding (ibid.).
women and relatives. Even though they are disqualified from testimony (Hilchot Edut 9:1).
those disqualified by the Sages for a transgression. Who committed transgressions that are rabbinic and were disqualified from testimony (see ibid. 10:3-4).
those disqualified for a transgression by the Torah. Who committed a transgression from the Torah (see ibid.).

where the get was validated by its signers. The court confirmed the signatures of the witnesses, and there is some basis for validity in this get, but it is disqualified because we worry that they were not appointed as agents (Yad Peshutah).
if one relied on it only on the words of a disqualified person... it is not a get. For there is no testimony besides theirs.
and he was healed. He recovered from his deafness.
and he became sane. He became of sound mind.
and he was freed. And through his freeing he became a convert and has the law of a Jew for all matters (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 12:17, 13:12).
it is void. For it was given to the agent while he was disqualified from agency.
and a woman may appoint an agent of receipt etc.. She has the power to do this, even though he does not receive the get from the husband's hand.

even though her courtyard acquires her get for her like an adult... it needs witnesses. Although the courtyard acquires for her from the exposition of the verse 'her hand' (see Hilchot Gezelah Va'avedah 17:10), and from the same exposition the agent of receipt was also included (above 5:1), nevertheless she does not appoint an agent, because appointing him needs witnesses.

and the husband said to him, 'I do not wish you to receive for her etc.'. The husband did not agree to give him the get as an agent of receipt, who receives in her place, but rather to bring her the get as an agent of carrying.
you are as she said. I agree to what the woman appointed you.
I appointed you only as an agent of bringing. I appointed you to be an agent of bringing, and not as you told the husband.

she is not divorced, for the agent uprooted the agency that she said etc.. From his saying that he is an agent of receipt, it seems that he does not agree to be an agent of bringing, to take the trouble to bring the get to her, but only to receive it for her. Therefore it turns out that he is not acting as the woman's agent, nor as the husband's agent, who relied on his words and did not appoint him.
rather he diminished it. The woman appointed him to be an agent fully filling her place, and he reduced his agency to bringing the get, and did not cancel it.
let this get be a deposit with you. She meant that he should receive the get for her.
she is doubtfully divorced etc.. It was not decided whether an agent of carrying can become an agent of receipt before completing his first agency (Babylonian Talmud Gittin 63b).
like the law of the husband with her. For even before the husband, the witnesses of delivery must read the get (above 1:19-22).
for he stands in his place. The agent fills the husband's place.
this is a doubtfully divorced woman. Like the law with the husband, in this case (above 1:21).
between him and her. Without witnesses.
this is valid. Like the law of the husband in such a case (above 1:16).
it is void even though it reached her hand. For the agency can be cancelled before it is carried out, and if he gave the get after the cancellation he does not divorce.

and anyone who cancels before others must cancel before two. That there be witnesses to the matter (Ramban, Gittin 32b), or so that there be publicity (Rashi and Tosafot there). However, the Sages forbade doing so for fear of mishap (below halakhah 26).

and even if he retracted within the time of speech and cancelled it... it is not cancelled. Even if the husband cancelled the get within the time in which one can say the words 'peace upon you, Rabbi' (Hilchot Shevu'ot 2:17), it is not cancelled. Although in most halakhic matters a person can retract his statement if such a time has not passed, in divorce and betrothal this rule does not apply (see Hilchot Ishut 7:22).
the husband was going about seeking the agent. The husband goes around looking for him.
and while he is going about and pursuing, the get reached her hand. While he was seeking the agent, the woman received the get.
and even though he was going about etc.. Because in practice he did not cancel it, and things in the heart are not things (Hilchot Ishut 8:2).
he said to ten, 'Write a get and give it to my wife'. And the law is that one writes and two sign, and one of them gives her the get (below 9:27).

he can cancel this one not in front of that one, even in front of two others. He tells one of them not to write and give, as the law of cancelling before the agent carrying the get (above halakhah 16). He may also say before two witnesses that he cancels the agency of writing and giving, as the law of cancelling not in the presence of the agent of carrying (ibid., Ma'aseh Rokeach).

and even if there were ten, once he cancelled before one, the get is void. The last sentence refers to both cases: whether in the agency of writing and giving or in the agency of carrying, if he cancelled for some of his agents, the get is void. The reason is that testimony that is partly void is void entirely (see Hilchot Edut 5:3), and likewise an agency that is partly void is void entirely (Ma'aseh Rokeach, and compare the explanation of the Maggid Mishneh cited in the poskim and opinions).

delivery of a moda'ah. Advance notice to witnesses that a particular act is being done against a person's will and will later be cancelled. This law applies in gittin as in all monetary law (see Hilchot Mekhirah chapter 10).
and any matter by which I cancel this moda'ah is void. And if he announced so, then even if he cancelled the moda'ah on the get, his moda'ah stands and the get is void.
if so, what is the remedy for this. How do we prevent the possibility of cancelling the get by moda'ah.
and he says 'yes'. Yes, that he agrees to their words.
and no... act of acquisition is needed. There is no need to do an act of acquisition that gives validity to the matter, but the announcement by itself suffices.
he may again divorce with it. He can use the same get.
for he did not cancel it as a get but as an agency. He cancelled the agent's appointment and not the validity of the get.
I do not want it. I do not wish it.

for this is not a language of cancelling but a language of informing of the truth of the matter. These expressions are not interpreted as an active statement of cancellation but as a description of an existing state.
a thing that is not so. Something that is not true, since no defect has yet been found in that get.
this get is void... it is doubtful. It was not decided whether to interpret it as a description of a past situation, or as cancellation.
blessed is the One who is good and does good. A blessing on good news (Hilchot Berakhot 10:3).
the get was not cancelled. For it was only implied from his words that he wants cancellation, and he did not explicitly cancel it (see above halakhah 17).
rebellion lashes. A liability of lashes by rabbinic law.

because he causes mamzerim etc.. For she might marry by mistake with this get, without knowing it is not valid. And if children are born to her from another man while she is still the first one's wife, they have the law of mamzerim, like all born of forbidden sexual relations (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 15:1).
we do not say perhaps the husband cancelled it. We do not generally worry about this, but assume he did not cancel it.
she must leave, and the child is a mamzer. She must be divorced from her second husband, since she is still married to the first.
and the husband left him sick... he gives it to her presuming he is alive. We do not worry that the husband died in the meantime, but assume he is still alive, as he was when the agent set out.
if he left him dying, most dying people die. If he was inclined to die when he left, we worry that he died, since most dying people do not recover, and he should not give her the get.
and a ship tossed at sea. That fell into a storm.
and one going out to be judged. To be tried, and perhaps a death sentence will be pronounced on him.
these are presumed alive. For they may have been saved from the danger, and we do not assume they died.
and a ship lost at sea. For which no possibility remains to save it (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Gittin 3:4).

we apply to them the stringencies of the living and the stringencies of the dead. We worry and rule stringently according to both possibilities, that he may be alive and may be dead (and see Hilchot Terumot 9:2).
the conditions of the ketubah. Obligations accompanying the main ketubah, such as the duty to heal her, redeem her and bury her (for the details of his obligations see Hilchot Ishut 12:2).
he is liable for her sustenance. For as long as she is his wife he is obligated in this.
and he does not know who his witnesses are. The agent does not know the witnesses signed on the get.

and even though we do not know his witnesses, she is divorced. For if the husband challenges the document, in the Land of Israel the witnesses are available to confirm it, as below halakhah 2. 2. It is validated by its signers. The court will check the authenticity of the signatures on it and confirm it (see Hilchot Edut 6:2).
his witnesses were not known at all. The signing witnesses are unknown, and their signatures cannot be confirmed.

she must leave, and the child is a mamzer, for she is not divorced. As long as there is no proof that the get is genuine, the woman remains presumed a married woman, and her child from another man is therefore a mamzer.
doubtfully divorced. Perhaps it would have been possible to validate the get had it not been lost.

and she intends to spoil her etc.. There is concern that out of hatred they would bring her a forged get so she would marry another on its basis, and thereby be forbidden to her husband (and see below 10:7).
her mother-in-law. Her husband's mother.
and her mother-in-law's daughter. Her husband's sister.
and her co-wife, even if the co-wife was married to another. Another wife of her husband, and even though they are no longer married to the same man, we assume she still hates her.

and her yevamah, even if she was her sister. The wife of her husband's brother, even if they were two sisters married to two brothers, so that she could not be taken in levirate marriage by her husband's brother (Hilchot Yibbum Vachalitzah 6:13; Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 2:9).
one who brings a get... in the Land of Israel and became ill etc.. For the law of one who brings a get outside the Land and became ill see below halakhah 20.
was compelled. Was forced for some reason not to fulfill his agency.
and he does not need witnesses to appoint an agent in their presence. For no witnesses are needed for an agent of carrying (as above 6:4).
even though the first agent died. For the agency comes by the husband's power and not by the agent's power (Babylonian Talmud Gittin 29b).
'in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed'. This testimony serves as a kind of validation of the get.

and even if its witnesses had gentile names, we do not worry about them. We do not suspect that the witnesses of the document are gentiles, since Jews outside the Land were accustomed to be called by gentile names too.

therefore even women who hate one another are believed etc.. Those same women were mentioned above, halakhah 3. And since the husband's challenge is not heeded, the concern that those women would come to spoil is nullified. 7. Even though he does not need. As explained above, halakhah 1.
and if the agent is not standing at the time of writing and signing. In a get brought from outside the Land.
and the agent may be one of the three etc.. For validation of documents is by three judges (see Hilchot Edut 6:1), and for validating the get the agent may be one of them (compare below halakhah 19).

and if it was not validated and was given to her, it is invalid. By the Sages' decree, as long as it is not known that it was written validly (as below halakhah 8), unlike gittin of the Land of Israel, which are presumed valid unless the husband challenges (below halakhah 24).
clear proof. Witnesses.
and the islands in the Great Sea within the boundary etc.. Small islands in the Mediterranean, in territory belonging to the Land of Israel.
and they will be explained in Hilchot Terumot. Hilchot Terumot 1:7-9.

and Babylon is like the Land of Israel for gittin. The law of gittin in the land of Babylon is as the laws of gittin of the Land of Israel, because there too there was a large and stable Jewish settlement.
its first part. The first part of the get.
a line. A row.
the sound of the quill. The sound of the quill, the noise of the writing instrument scraping on the paper.

even if he was the second witness. And his signature is validated by his own testimony. In this situation, although there is testimony on both signatures, the get will not be given to her, because both signatures must be validated in the same way - both by the testimony 'it was signed in my presence', or both by validation of the get by two witnesses.

for his agents are his witnesses etc.. For the agents of the get are fit to be themselves the witnesses of the divorce (see above 2:2), and are afterwards believed to testify that she was divorced, and therefore the husband cannot claim forgery (as above, halakhah 8).
for the get comes out from under the hand of both. For both are his agents.
but when it does not come out from under their hand. But only one of them is the husband's agent.
between him and her. Between the two of them, without witnesses to the fact that he said 'it was written in my presence and signed in my presence'.
this is invalid etc.. As above, halakhah 7. 18. Who became mute. Who became dumb, unable to speak.
the blind man. Blind.
a sighted one. Able to see.
when the agent is fit for testimony. And the woman and the blind man are disqualified from testimony (Hilchot Edut 9:1).

for they did not say before two... that the witness becomes a judge in a matter that is by their words. For in matters that are by the Sages' enactment, they were lenient that even a witness becomes like a judge (see above halakhah 7).

the agent became ill or was compelled, he comes to the court etc.. For in gittin outside the Land he cannot appoint another agent (as above halakhah 4), since the agent must say 'in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed', and one who comes on his behalf cannot testify so.
but if the get was validated by its signers etc.. Then it has the law of gittin of the Land of Israel, in which an agent appoints an agent himself (above halakhah 4).
anyone who appoints an agent. A man or a woman.
and likewise the agent appoints an agent. As explained above (halakhah 4).
and said to her, 'Behold you are an agent' etc.. That he did not give her the get in order to divorce her, but only as an agency.
she is believed to say before them, 'in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed'. For she is not suspected of lying in this matter (and see below 12:15).
where the husband stipulated this condition with her. When the husband told her the condition mentioned in the previous halakhah.

we do not worry that she forged it, for she does not spoil for herself. There is no concern that the woman brought a forged get, since if the matter becomes known she would be forbidden to her second husband and her children from him would be mamzerim (below 10:7).
until there is a challenger there. As long as there is no challenge against it.
for if one were to be concerned about these matters and the like. If one had to worry about every possible problem with a get.
perhaps he nullified it and afterwards gave it. He cancelled the get itself, so as not to divorce (above 6:21).
or perhaps invalid witnesses signed on it, making it like a forgery on its face. That it is proven from the get itself that it is forged (above 1:7).
or perhaps it was not written for her sake. Not for the sake of this man and this woman (above 3:1). All these disqualifications are not apparent in the get itself, unless it is investigated.

for the laws of prohibitions are not like the laws of monetary matters. In prohibitions we rely on a presumption, whereas in monetary law one cannot extract money without proof (and see Hilchot Avadim 7:2).

all the laws of conditions. The laws that apply to all conditions, whether for divorce and betrothal or for sales and other monetary law (see Hilchot Ishut 6:1, and see there 6:14). "These are the four requirements of every condition: that it be doubled, that its 'yes' precede its 'no', that the condition precede the act, and that the condition be one that can be fulfilled. If any one of them is missing, the condition is void, as if there were no condition at all, and she is immediately betrothed or divorced..." (there 6:2; and later in the chapter these four requirements are explained).
the husband may. The husband is permitted to.

and if the husband died... before the condition was fulfilled, she is not divorced. The husband and the get must both exist at the time, because the divorce takes effect only when the condition is fulfilled.

and if she remarried, she does not have to leave. For the divorce already began from the moment the get was handed over, though it is not yet complete, and therefore she is no longer considered a married woman (Yad Peshutah; and see below 9:1, 5).
she no longer has it in her power to fulfil it. That she is no longer able to fulfil the condition of the get (see examples below, halachot 22-23).

from now or from today... on condition that. These are conditions of a different type, and in such wording there is no need for the laws of conditions that apply to an "if" condition (see Hilchot Ishut 6:17).
and we are not concerned that it may not be fulfilled, etc.. For she has the ability to fulfil it, and she will be divorced from the moment the get was given.
because she is not ashamed to have relations in their presence. She is not embarrassed to have marital relations in their presence.

perhaps she had relations and the get was nullified. For we assume that if she had relations it was for the sake of betrothal, since a person does not make his act of intercourse an act of licentiousness.
as will be explained in these laws. Below 10:18.
not that he says: Write a get for my wife conditionally, etc.. Rather, the get must be written for the sake of a complete divorce.
the main body of the get. The essential part of the get: the name of the man and the name of the woman, the date of the get, and the words "you are permitted to any man" (above 3:17).
even if he wrote: on condition of such and such. This is a better condition than an "except" condition (see the next halacha).

it is a doubtful divorce, since he retained a right in the body of the get itself. Because the essence of the get was not written unconditionally but conditionally, it is doubtful whether there is a "severance" here (see above 1:3).
except to a certain man. Apart from a certain man.
a gentile, a slave, or one forbidden to her as a forbidden relation, etc.. Betrothal does not take effect with them (Hilchot Ishut 4:12, 4:15), so he has left no restriction on her on his account.
from those liable under a prohibition. Betrothal does take effect with them (there, halacha 14).
even if he is a minor. And his betrothal is not valid betrothal (there, halacha 7).
he reserved in the get, and this is not a severance. He left some of the marital prohibitions that the get did not release, so the get does not completely sever the bond between them.

he was her sister's husband. He stipulated that the get would not permit her to her sister's husband. She is forbidden to him as a forbidden relation, unless her sister dies (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 2:9).
not in the usual way. Intercourse from behind, through the rectum.
from the annulment of your vows. That the husband is able to annul his wife's vows (Hilchot Nedarim, chapters 11-13).
eating terumah. That the wife of a kohen is permitted to eat terumah (Hilchot Terumot 6:3).
he said to her: You are permitted to Reuven. After first saying "except for Reuven and Shimon."
he said to her: You are permitted to Shimon. It is doubtful whether he meant to include Reuven too and said Shimon because that was where he ended his words, or whether he meant Shimon specifically.
in gittin we write: from today and forever. As set out in the text of the get (cited above 4:12).
all the days of your life. All your life.
for this is not a severance. For the restriction applies permanently.
it is not a get. Because the condition remains in force all the days of her life.
the get is retroactively void. It is annulled from the time it was given, since it became clear that it never took effect.
she committed adultery with him, etc.. If she committed adultery with the man he excluded but did not marry him, the adultery does not nullify the get.
she married another before marrying him, the get is void. For the condition was not fulfilled, since she did not marry that particular man.

and she requires a get from the second. From the second husband, even though his betrothal does not take effect with her, so that people will not say that a married woman leaves her husband without a get (below 10:4).
and the paper. The body of the document of the get.
it is a get. For a gift given on condition that it be returned is a valid gift (see Hilchot Zechiyah u-Matanah 3:9), and she acquired the body of the get.
for he stipulated other conditions before writing the main body. In this case the get is void (above, halacha 4).
and again stipulated another condition with her. For as long as the condition has not been fulfilled, the husband can change it, as above, halacha 1.
that she serve. That she wait on.

and one of the first and one of the last do not combine. One of the first witnesses does not combine with one of the later witnesses to testify that there was a condition in the get, since these are two different conditions.
the condition of two hundred has already been nullified. Because both concern the same matter, and the latter condition contradicts the first.
that she do this thing without specifying. That he did not state explicitly for how long.
and that is within twenty-four months. From the day of his birth (below 11:26).
she completes the time he specified. She fulfils the condition for the entire period the husband specified.
from here. From today.
of his own will. Voluntarily.
and she did not give, she is not divorced. And giving to the heirs does not help (see the next halacha).
and the get is not void, since he did not set a time. Therefore in principle, were it not for the husband's absence, it could still be fulfilled.
even if the get was lost or torn. For the later existence of the get is not important in a condition of "on condition that" (above, halacha 1).

she is divorced, etc.. Since a conditional divorce begins from the time the get was given (below 9:1), she is considered divorced, but the fulfilment of the condition remains pending without resolution, and therefore she is not exempt from chalitzah (Rabbi Y. Kafih).
even if she gave him a thousand times its value. Even if she paid a thousand times its worth, but did not give the vessel itself.
and another betrothed her. But she has not yet married the second.
and if it was not fulfilled and the get was void. For example, if he stipulated that she give him two hundred zuz by a certain time
,. and the time passed and she did not give.
for betrothal does not take effect with her. For betrothal does not take effect with a married woman, or with any of those liable to karet.
but if she married... she requires a get from the second. By rabbinic enactment, so that people will not say a married woman leaves her husband without a get (see below 10:4).
as we have explained. Above, halacha 13.
that she is divorced when the time he set arrives. In an ordinary condition, the divorce process is completed by the fulfilment of the condition (see above 8:1).
he has divorced. For the divorce process began with the giving of the get.
he must double his statement. That if the condition is fulfilled she will be divorced, and if not she will not be divorced.
the laws of conditions that we have explained. Hilchot Ishut 6:1-2.
at the side of the public domain. In a place beside the public domain where the public does not walk, a place where the get is safeguarded.
as we have explained. Above 8:1.
as we have explained. That if she placed the get at the side of the public domain, she is divorced (above, halacha 3).
he has not divorced at all. Because he did not say explicitly that if she gives, she will be divorced.

and it is not dependent on an act. He did not make the taking effect of the get depend on an act as stated above, halacha 4, and since he did not say "this is your get" (but "this is not a get") or "you are divorced," there is no divorce here.
one who wishes to divorce conditionally, etc.. So that she will be divorced even if the get is not in her possession, like a get for which a time was set (above, halacha 5).
states this matter in the language of a condition. He phrases his words as a condition.
or says to her, etc.. For in a "from now" condition there is no need to double the condition
,. and one who says "on condition that" is like one who says "from now" (see Hilchot Ishut 6:17).
for there is no duress in gittin. The condition is not cancelled in a get, even if duress prevented him from meeting the condition (unlike a monetary condition, see Hilchot Mechirah 19:5-7).
even though he revealed his intention. Even though it is clear that he does not wish to divorce her.
when thirty days pass from before her. That they will not meet for a month.
and he kept going and coming, going and coming. Going and returning, and meeting her each time.
when he goes and stays thirty days. During which they will not meet at all.

even though he went and came within thirty days, etc.. Although he returned within thirty days, we are not concerned that he had relations with her and that the get is now "old" and invalid (above 3:5, below 10:18), since they were not alone together. And when the condition is completed she will be divorced by it.

we are concerned that he appeased her... and nullified the get. For the condition was originally made for the woman's benefit, to prevent the husband from being away for a long time. Here we are concerned that he asked her to waive the condition for him, she agreed, and thereby he nullified the get. But if he stipulated that she would be believed to claim that he did not appease her, he cannot claim that he nullified it.

conditions that depend on her will; if she wished and waived them and her husband nullified the get. Conditions that are for the woman's benefit, which she can waive for her husband, and he then nullify the get. [Some manuscripts read: "and if she wished and nullified them, the get is void."]
familiar with her. Accustomed to her.

she may not marry in place of a yavam. If the deceased has a brother and no children, the widow is forbidden to marry others because of the mitzvah of yibbum (Hilchot Yibbum va-Chalitzah 1:1-2), whereas a divorcee is permitted. Such a woman is not treated as divorced as long as the condition has not been fulfilled, even though it is perfectly clear that it will be fulfilled at the end of the time he set (and see above 8:22).
he has said nothing. His statement has no effect.

for "if I die" can mean after death and can mean from now. His words can be interpreted to mean that the get takes effect from the moment he dies, or from the moment of speaking. As long as nothing proves otherwise, his words are interpreted in their first sense (as in the next halacha).
and when he dies she will be divorced. Retroactively from the time of speaking.
when the sun rises. When the sun shines; this is a get dependent on time, which takes effect only when the time arrives (above, halacha 1).
on condition that the sun rises. In such a condition, once the condition is fulfilled she is divorced retroactively from the time the get was given (above 8:1).
that if the sun rises it will be a get, etc.. In such a condition, the divorce is completed only when the condition is fulfilled (above, halachot 1, 5; 8:1).
a seriously ill person. A dangerously ill person who is about to die.
and he recovered. He got well.
he cannot retract. Although it seems that he meant to divorce her only on the condition that he die (for the wording of the get that allows a sick person to retract, see below, halacha 20).
for his get is not like his gift. For in his gift, if he recovers the transfer is cancelled, since it was made only out of fear that he would die (Hilchot Zechiyah u-Matanah 8:14).

for if you say he may retract, etc.. If the law for a get were that he could retract if he recovered, like a gift, people would err and say that when he said he divorces her after death, the get is valid.
it is not a get. For he did not die of that illness but from something else.

she is a doubtfully divorced woman. It is uncertain whether the condition means that he not recover from his illness, or that he die of the illness; and he did not die of that illness but from something else, so the condition was not fulfilled.
and he recovered and walked in the marketplace. He grew stronger and walked in the street.
we estimate. We assess.
he passed from one illness to another. He fell ill with a different illness and died of it.
that he not be alone with her. Lest he have relations with her and nullify the get.
as we have explained. Above 8:2.
so that she will not fall before a yavam. So that she is divorced and not a widow, so that she does not require yibbum or chalitzah from his brother.
and if he recovered, she will not be divorced. And he wants the get not to take effect if he recovers.

and he did not want to divorce her from now, etc.. For in many respects a "from now" conditional divorce takes effect immediately upon giving the get (see above 8:1), and thoughts about this might disturb his mind.
after he writes the main body. Because one does not write a condition before writing the main body of the get (above 8:4).
and the yes comes before the no. "If I die" comes before "if I do not die."
and he should not open his mouth first with misfortune. Therefore he first says "if I do not die."

she is doubtfully divorced, for most women, it is a benefit, etc.. We are concerned that this is a benefit to her and not a detriment, since most women prefer not to be subject to yibbum. The rule is: "We act for a person's benefit in his absence, but we cannot impose a liability on him except in his presence" (compare above 5:2).
we write after the time he set and give it to her. And we do not say that he meant that they should write it within the time and give it after the time.
after the Shevu'a. After the Shemitah year.

but only until a year after the Shevu'a. Only the year following the Shemitah. It may not be delayed longer, because the phrase "after the Shevu'a" means immediately after it, without an additional unit of time following it (Yad Peshutah).
after the Sabbath of the second month. From the departure of the first Sabbath that falls in the next month (ibid.).
after two Sabbaths of the second month. From the departure of the second Sabbath that falls in the next month (Yad Peshutah).
when he was alone with her the get became invalid. For we are concerned that she had relations and was thereby betrothed, and she requires a get out of doubt (below 10:18; Yad Peshutah).
all the more so in this case, where it was not written. Because he cancelled their agency.
through. On behalf of.
in the presence of. In the presence of.
he counted them. He enumerated them.
it is as if he said: All of you sign. That everyone he counted must sign.
and the rest because of the condition. The signature of the rest does not have the status of testimony on the get, but only fulfils the husband's condition.
if the rest were invalid... it is valid. Whereas if their signatures had the status of testimony, the get would be invalid (above 1:17, 25).

lest they say an invalid witness is valid in the testimony of other documents, etc.. The law for other documents is that all signers are considered a single testimony if they sat together to sign, and if one of them is invalid, the document is void (Hilchot Edut 5:6).

and they did not validate it in a get with many witnesses, etc.. In a get they were lenient, permitting invalid people to sign the get (because of the condition), because the witnesses of delivery are the main ones, and the witnesses of signature are only a rabbinic enactment (above 1:15).
each one of you shall write a get, etc.. Each one of them is qualified for this. They enacted this so that it should not seem that he means all of them (above, halachot 26-27).
lest two testify, etc.. Since not all of the signers are present there, only two of them will sign, and the woman will think it valid, even though the condition was not fulfilled.
and among them were a father and his son. They are not qualified to sign the get together, because they are relatives and are disqualified from testifying together (Hilchot Edut 13:1).

for a person makes a son an agent in place of the father. A person appoints his son as agent even when his father is present, and we need not be concerned that he specifically intended to appoint the father out of respect for him.
what should they do. If they gave her the get themselves.
and my teachers ruled, etc.. See the rulings and opinions.
and gave it to the husband without witnesses. Without witnesses having signed on it.
give this get to my wife in the presence of witnesses. Witnesses of delivery without witnesses of signature (see above 1:18).
she is doubtfully divorced. Because there is no proof that the get was given at the husband's instruction.

for the agent is not believed to permit a forbidden relation, even though he is one witness, except because of the witnesses' signatures. Generally the validity of the get and the agent's credibility in bringing it derive from the witnesses' signing on the get, which is proof that the get was given at the husband's instruction.
as we have explained. Above 7:24. And here there are no witnesses of signature.
she is divorced. For there is proof that the get was given at the husband's instruction (Yad Peshutah).
