and gave it to her in another place, it is not a get. For the husband said to give it to her in that place, so he was particular about it, and if he did not do as he said, he is not his agent.
valid, because he was merely showing him the place. The husband specified her location to help the agent find her, but was not particular that it be given to her specifically there.
in the upper room. On the second floor.
within the time. Before that day the husband mentioned arrived.

and likewise the woman who said, etc.. In agency to receive a get, the agent receives the get in place of the woman herself, and by this act she is divorced (see above 6:1-4), so deviations in carrying it out void the agency itself. Whereas bringing the get to the woman is only an act of transport, so there is no insistence on the place of receipt (Ran on the Rif, Gittin 31b).
he may send it through another. He is permitted to appoint another as agent to give the woman the get (above 7:4).
he may not send it through another. For he does not want this item deposited in the hands of another (below, halacha 37).

and the woman went out to meet the agent... she is divorced. Although initially he should not send it through another, nevertheless the husband's requirement was fulfilled, to take the item and then give the get.

he transgressed the husband's words in something about which people are generally particular. For the husband wanted her to give the item before receiving the get, so that the get would be given in exchange for that item (see Rashi, Gittin 29b).
for he does not want his deposit to be in the hands of another. The husband does not want a third person to guard the item for him, only the agent he appointed (Hilchot Sechirut 1:4).
and if he sent it through another, it is a get. For the giving of the get was not made conditional on giving the item.

he is an agent who was not appointed for divorce. Although the husband originally wished to appoint him as the agent for the get, and only because he did not know her told him to give it to another, he is not considered an agent for divorce, since in the end he was not appointed to divorce.
he may send it through another. To give it after thirty days have passed.
when her husband was not with her in the country. So there is no concern that he came within this time and appeased her, and nullified the get (above, halacha 9).
or she was being divorced from betrothal. He is not familiar with her, and we are not concerned that he appeased her (ibid.).

we are concerned that perhaps he appeased her. Since he delayed the time of giving the get, we are concerned that he had not made up his mind to divorce her and left himself the possibility of appeasing her and cancelling the get (Meiri, Gittin 29b).
but the one who gives the get. The first agent himself.
and we are concerned for her. Lest he appeased her.
as we have explained. Above, halacha 9.
she must leave and the child is a mamzer. For it was born of the prohibition of a married woman, which is among the forbidden relations (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 15:1-2).
she is not forbidden to him as a divorcee. A divorcee is forbidden to a kohen (ibid. 17:1), but here she was not divorced at all.
by their enactment. By rabbinic enactment.
and this is called the "scent of a get". This case is so called because of its resemblance to divorce.
and she is disqualified thereby from the priesthood by Torah law. For by Torah law the get is valid.
and she is under her husband. Even while she is married to her second husband.
and the husband was scrupulous. In a case where the second husband was careful in mitzvot and did not want to be married in a manner that is not ideal.
lest he cast a slur on his children. For if he divorces her, people will think he divorced her by law and not out of piety, and they will say that his children from this woman are mamzerim.
a possible mamzer. Who is forbidden to enter the assembly by rabbinic enactment (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 15:21).
and he wanted to take her back. That same first husband.
and he need not renew the marriage, etc.. For the bond between them was not completely severed (and see Hilchot Ishut 18:25).
she requires a get from the second husband by rabbinic enactment. For by Torah law no get is needed, since the second's betrothal does not take effect with her, for she is still a married woman.

so that people will not say a married woman leaves without a get. Because she appeared to be properly married to the second (since the first gave her a get), and if she were allowed to leave the second without a get, people might think a woman can be divorced without a get.

even though she had relations inadvertently, etc.. Although generally a woman is not forbidden to her husband if she had relations inadvertently (Hilchot Ishut 24:19), here she is forbidden because the situation resembles his divorcee who married another, whom the first may not take back (below 11:12).
and afterwards her husband came. And from this it became clear that the testimony was false.
whether he was deaf... his betrothal is not complete betrothal. Rather it is a rabbinic enactment (Hilchot Ishut 4:9).

she must leave both of them, etc.. We do not consider whether Torah-level betrothal took effect in the first or the second betrothal, for all the prohibitions here are a rabbinic decree in a situation where she appears married to two men.

if a woman was betrothed. To another man, but has not yet married him. There was a condition in the betrothal which was not fulfilled. Conditions in betrothal are common (see Hilchot Ishut chapters 6-8), but not in marriage (ibid. 7:23).

neither the first nor the second husband is entitled to what she finds, etc.. Neither of them receives the rights of a husband, who acquires a lost item his wife finds and the earnings of her work (Hilchot Ishut 12:3) and annuls her vows (Hilchot Nedarim 11-13).
and all the produce. Of her nichsei melug (property retained by her).
from the conditions of the ketubah. Detailed in Hilchot Ishut 12:2.

and anything of her property that wore out or was lost. Which in an ordinary case the husband must restore as it was when they married (see ibid. 16:1-2). If the wife committed adultery, he need not restore to her the difference in value (ibid. 24:10).
a mamzer by rabbinic law. Because it appeared as if she had married the second (above, halacha 4).
what she took is not taken from her. Just as what came into the husband's hands permissibly is not taken from him (Yerushalmi, Yevamot 10:1).
and all these ways apply to her. All the details of the halacha stated in the previous halacha apply in this case too.

and he heard that she died, and married her sister, and afterwards it became known that she had not died. For a man's wife's sister is forbidden to him during his wife's lifetime, but not after her death (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 2:9).

but if his married wife went, etc.. In this law of the prohibition of her sister, there is a difference between the case where he betrothed a woman and the case where he also married her, as will be explained in the next halacha.
and why did they require the sister of his betrothed to have a get. For betrothal does not take effect with forbidden relations, so what is the difference between the previous two halachot?

lest they say there was a condition in the betrothal, etc.. Those who see him marrying the sister of his betrothed will think that the first betrothal was conditional and was cancelled by the condition, so that he married the second permissibly. But if he marries his wife's sister, they will not assume there was a condition (above, halacha 6), but will know that it was because of the false report that her sister had died, and that in truth betrothal did not take effect with her.
and he erred and gave, etc.. Because of the error the get was never given to the woman, and there was no divorce.
the receipt. A receipt, which the woman gives her husband upon receiving her ketubah.
and the get came out from under the man's hand. It was found with him, and so it became known that it was not given to the woman.
and let him give her the get in our presence. Let him divorce her with this get before the court.

rather she is presumed to be a divorcee and the get fell from her hand. We do not believe the husband to remove her from the presumption of being a divorcee in such a case, but assume that the get was originally given to her and reached his hand in another way.
a bad name. A suspicion based on promiscuity, but without complete testimony (Hilchot Ishut 24:15).
loose with vows. She makes many vows and prohibits things to herself (see ibid. 12:24).

he informed her: it is because of this that I am divorcing you, in order to discipline her. The husband must inform the woman that the divorce is because of her conduct, so that she will return to the right path.
like one who divorces conditionally. As though he had stipulated that she would be divorced only if she was found not to be behaving properly.
therefore we say to him: Resolve in your heart to divorce her, etc.. And after such agreement it is clear that this is not a conditional divorce.
an ailonit. A woman whose sexual development is defective (Hilchot Ishut 2:6).
who bleeds at every time of intercourse. A woman who bled during intercourse three consecutive times, whose husband is obligated to divorce her (Hilchot Ishut 25:8; Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 4:21).
and said: It was written in my presence and signed in my presence. Thereby validating the get and permitting the woman to remarry (above 7:5).
for we are concerned that he has his eye on her. That he desires her, and testified falsely in order to permit her to himself.
and likewise one witness who testified to a woman that her husband died. Who is believed to permit her to remarry (below 12:15).
the sage who forbade the woman to her husband by a vow. The woman vowed not to benefit from her husband, and the sage forbade them to live together because he could not find a way to release the vow.

one suspected regarding a maidservant... he may not marry her. One suspected of having relations with a maidservant or a gentile woman may not marry her, so that the suspicion will not be confirmed (for a similar law see Hilchot Sotah 2:13).

and likewise a gentile or slave who had relations with a Jewish woman... he may not marry her. They are penalized for the transgression they committed. Or the reason is "lazut sefatayim" (a bad appearance), lest people say the conversion was done for the sake of the marriage (see Bavli Yevamot 24b and Rabbenu Chananel there).
and all of them who had wives. All those listed in the previous halacha, who were married at the time they did the act that led to the woman's permission.

or they were divorced and the wives were the ones who induced their husbands to divorce them. That the divorce was initiated by the wife, in which case there is no concern that he is marrying her because he set his eye on her while he was married.
these women are permitted to marry them initially. There is no longer concern that the permission was granted for the sake of their marriage, since she married another.
and let him come close to the chalitzah. Let a person join the testimony of the chalitzah, for there is a mitzvah in this (see Yad Peshutah).
from the witnesses of her annulment. The witnesses who testified that the woman annulled her marriage to her husband (explained at length in the next chapter).
to one of the judges before whom she performed chalitzah. For chalitzah is performed before three judges (Hilchot Yibbum va-Chalitzah 4:1).

for we are concerned only about the testimony of one. Only where the testimony of a single witness is accepted, as explained in the previous halachot, is there concern that he has his eye on her and lies to permit her to himself. But the witnesses and judges are two or three.
a person should keep away from testifying to an annulment. He should try not to testify to an annulment.

she is presumed to have taken her back, and he had relations for the sake of betrothal. Since she was his wife, we assume that he had relations with her for the sake of betrothal and not for licentiousness.
even if they saw him give her money. Although he paid her and it looks like licentiousness.
and this is only if the two witnesses were as one. That they both saw it together.

and they are both the witnesses of seclusion and the witnesses of intercourse. The witnesses who testify to the seclusion are considered witnesses to the intercourse, though they did not see the intercourse itself.
as we have explained. Hilchot Ishut 3:5.
he is not familiar with her. He is not accustomed to her, so there is no concern that he had relations with her.
it is a presumption that a person does not make his intercourse an act of licentiousness. Rather, he has relations for the sake of betrothal.

and they added... until they ruled that one who has a son by his maidservant, etc.. A man who had relations with his Canaanite maidservant and she bore a son: that son is not considered his son and does not take his lineage, and if he dies without other children his wife requires yibbum (Hilchot Yibbum va-Chalitzah 1:4). But those Geonim ruled to be concerned that perhaps he is like his son, and she should not enter yibbum but perform chalitzah out of doubt.

and some of them ruled that he certainly freed her, etc.. Because of this presumption, we should assume that he freed the maidservant and she is like a convert, and if he has offspring from her and dies, his wife is not subject to yibbum or chalitzah at all.
far... from the ways of ruling, etc.. These are not a correct halachic ruling.
one who betroths conditionally and had relations without specifying. See Hilchot Ishut 7:23.

and it is regarding his wife that his presumption is that he does not make his intercourse an act of licentiousness, etc.. Only with her is there a certain assumption that he had relations for the sake of betrothal. And it need not be said

regarding a maidservant or a gentile woman who is not eligible for betrothal. . with whom betrothal does not take effect (Hilchot Ishut 4:15), that he certainly did not intend it for the sake of betrothal.
who was presumed to be a married woman. That this was known to the public.
they spread the word. They publicize the rumor.
we do not worry about her. And she is presumed to be married (and see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 17:19).
and the rumor was established in court. Witnesses testified to it before a court. For any rumor that was not established in court, we do not take into account.
for she is betrothed out of doubt, as we have explained. For the law is that we are concerned for her betrothal, Hilchot Ishut 9:22.

for a rumor forbade her and a rumor permitted her. Since she is considered betrothed and forbidden to others because of the rumor, the rumor also has the force to establish her as divorced and permit her to others.
a matter of indecency. Immodest conduct (Bavli Gittin 90a).
and it is not proper for him to hasten to send away his first wife. Who became bound to him in companionship and covenant.
of bad character. In her traits and conduct.
he may divorce her with a get. Even though she has no understanding, for a man can divorce his wife without her consent (above 1:2).
became insane. Went mad.
so that it not be ownerless for the licentious. For immorality.
and we do not obligate him for the rest of her clothing and conjugal rights. Although he does not divorce her, he is exempt from his personal obligations toward her.
and he is not obligated to heal her or redeem her. If she falls ill or is taken captive (ibid. 14:17-18).
one does not marry a minor girl. For this is not proper for several reasons (see Hilchot Ishut 3:19, 10:16; Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 21:18).
an orphaned minor girl. Who is not under her father's authority, and the Sages enacted that she may marry on her own.
she may annul her marriage and leave. She declares her refusal to continue her marriage, thereby cancelling it.
as we have explained. Hilchot Ishut 4:7-8.

a minor girl whose father married her off and who was widowed or divorced while a minor is like an orphan in her father's lifetime. For when her father married her off she left his authority, and once she was widowed or divorced she is in her own authority, like an orphan (ibid. 3:12). 2. Her marriage is by rabbinic enactment. The Sages enacted that she may marry, though she has no betrothal by Torah law (Hilchot Ishut 4:9).

so that they will not refrain from marrying her. Because she could always annul her marriage. But a minor girl annuls only while she is a minor, so they will not refrain from marrying her for that reason.

so she may annul against the yavam. If her husband dies, she can annul her bond with his brother who is to perform yibbum, severing the connection between them, and she needs neither yibbum nor chalitzah.
her betrothal is itself her annulment. Her very betrothal to the second is considered an annulment of the first, and she need not annul explicitly.
na'arah. A girl twelve years and one day old who has grown two hairs (Hilchot Ishut 2:1).
until it is known that she is an ailonit. A woman whose sexual development is defective, which is known by special signs (see ibid. 2:4-6).
and she does not require examination for the annulment, etc.. For we assume that if she reached the age of na'arah she has already grown two hairs.
and therefore she requires a get out of doubt. And she does not leave by annulment, lest at the time of intercourse she was a na'arah and acquired to him by Torah law.

and if she annulled after being examined and was betrothed to another, she requires a get out of doubt from him. From her second husband, if the first wishes to remain with her, lest she had developed signs before being betrothed to the second, and was acquired to the first by Torah law.
and the child is a possible mamzer from both of them. For it is uncertain whether she was married by Torah law to this one or to that one.
she cannot annul, since she has grown up. For a na'arah cannot annul (above, halacha 4).
and she requires a get by rabbinic enactment, since he did not have relations with her, etc.. Since she can no longer annul, she needs a get to leave him.
for they are by rabbinic enactment. As above, halacha 1.
the second's betrothal takes effect with her. Since she was betrothed to the first only by rabbinic law.
and if the first divorced, the second may marry her. The second is permitted to marry her, since by Torah law she was never married to the first.

lest they say he took back his divorcee after she was betrothed. For it appears as if he took back his divorcee after she was betrothed to another, which is forbidden by the Torah (below, halacha 12).
to a woman who heard that her husband died, etc.. See above 10:5.
and the child of the second is not a mamzer. Because the first's marriage is valid only by rabbinic law.
and if the first had relations with her before the second divorced, the child is a mamzer. For she is the wife of the second by Torah law.
who is a minor girl, etc.. For a similar halacha see Hilchot Ishut 4:7.
according to the maturity of her mind. The degree of her understanding.
if she knows how to safeguard her betrothal, etc.. To guard the item or money, and to understand its importance as betrothal.
and the date. The fruit of the date palm.
a foolish one. A silly girl.
without her consent. Without her agreement.
even if there were guests... and she stands and serves them drinks. Even though she behaves as his wife.
and none of the laws of a get of divorce. Which were detailed above 1:1.
and we do not write the forms of the get in it, etc.. We do not write it in the wording of the get, so that it will not resemble a divorce get.
like a court record. It is for evidence only of the annulment that took place, and is not like a divorce get, whose giving brings about the divorce.
one who saw her annul. In front of witnesses.
he may. He is permitted to.
even though they do not know them. For those before whom she annulled knew them.
on such and such day of the week. On a certain day of the week.
in the year such and such of the era of so and so. The year count customary in that place (see above 1:27).

and now I have revealed, etc.. Translation: and now I have disclosed my mind before you that I do not want him and I will not stay with him. And we examined this woman so-and-so, and it became clear to us that she is still a minor, and we wrote and signed and gave it to her as a proof and clear evidence.
and we examined this woman so-and-so. For the method of examination see Hilchot Ishut 2:20.

as it is said: Her first husband cannot. And the continuation of the verse: "who sent her away, take her again to be his wife after she has been defiled, for that is an abomination before the Lord, and you shall not bring sin upon the land that the Lord your God gives you as an inheritance."
she committed adultery. That she had relations licentiously.
her becoming another man's, that is the betrothal, etc.. Her very being his wife is what forbids her, not the intercourse.
and she has been defiled. That she committed adultery while a married woman.

unless she was the wife of an Israelite who was raped. She is not forbidden to her husband if she was raped. But the wife of a kohen is forbidden even if she was raped (Hilchot Ishut 24:21; Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 18:7).

warning and seclusion. Her husband warned her not to be alone with a certain man, and afterwards they saw that she was alone with him; she is forbidden to her husband until she is examined with the bitter waters (Hilchot Sotah 1:1-2).
as we have explained. Above 2:17.
and needless to say to a person of sound mind. Whose betrothal is complete betrothal.

she is permitted to return to her sound-minded husband. For her betrothal to a deaf-mute is not Torah-level, and is not considered complete betrothal (see Hilchot Ishut 4:9), and with respect to the sound-minded man she is not considered his divorcee who married another.
she is not divorced from him, etc.. She does not have the status of a divorcee, but as if there had been no connection between them.

she is permitted to his relatives and he is permitted to her female relatives. Unlike the law of divorce, where they remain forbidden to each other's relatives as they were during the marriage (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 2:1, 7).
but one who divorces... she is forbidden to return to the first because she left him by a get. And she appears to be his divorcee.
even though she left the last by annulment. For her annulment of the second does not cancel the get from the first marriage.

for she appears as his daughter-in-law at the time his son died. She had been married to his son who died, and though by strict law the annulment cancelled the marriage and the prohibition from the outset, they decreed it because of appearances.
therefore, etc.. Since she is permitted to the other relatives.
except for the day she was divorced, etc.. The day of divorce and the day of betrothal are not counted within the ninety days.
so that it be known whether she is pregnant or not pregnant. For after ninety days the fetus is discernible.
for he is not alone with her since he wrote it for her. So that it not have the status of an old get (as explained above 3:5).
divorced or widowed from betrothal. For during betrothal the husband was not yet permitted to have relations with her, and there is no concern that she is pregnant.
even if her husband was overseas or ill, etc.. For in such cases everyone knows that he did not have relations with her.
in order to distinguish, etc.. To know whether she conceived before she converted or afterwards, which matters for the laws of family relationship (see for example Hilchot Yibbum va-Chalitzah 1:8).
a beautiful woman. A gentile woman taken captive in war whom he wishes to marry, who has special laws (see Hilchot Melachim 8:2-6).
thirty days for her own benefit. That she agree to leave her religion and convert, after which he is permitted to marry her (ibid. 8:5).
for the benefit of the child. To determine when she conceived.
they decreed only for a divorcee. And not for one who annulled, since there is no situation of annulment for an adult woman capable of conceiving.
she guards herself so as not to become pregnant. For she does not want her adultery revealed, and tries to avoid conceiving.
raped or seduced. They too try to avoid conceiving.
one who married in error, etc.. For example, one who was betrothed to one man and married another because of a mix-up.
we excommunicate him. We punish him with excommunication, which is ostracism and social isolation (see Hilchot Talmud Torah chapter 7).
if he betrothed and fled, we do not excommunicate him. The distress of his flight is a punishment for him, and there is no need to excommunicate him (Maggid Mishneh).
married. Took in marriage.
we separate them. We separate them from one another.
and let him stay. He remains, and need not divorce her.

lest the milk be spoiled, and he does not take care to heal the milk... when she becomes pregnant. The quality of the milk could be impaired if she becomes pregnant again, and since the husband is not the baby's father, he does not take care to provide her with things that improve the milk's quality, and the baby would be harmed.
who weaned him. Who stopped nursing him.
she may not marry. Lest she wean him in order to be permitted to marry, though the baby is not capable of it, and endanger him.
and we are not concerned that she might kill him. For no sane woman would do so in order to be permitted to marry (Bavli Ketubot 60b).
if he transgressed and married... he must divorce with a get. In order to separate them absolutely (see Yad Peshutah).
even if he was a kohen. Who is forbidden to take back his divorcee.
and after some time he came. After twenty-four months.
if he betrothed... we do not force him to divorce. Since they do not live together in any case until he marries her.
for the mouth that forbade is the mouth that permitted. Since she is forbidden only by her own words, she is believed to permit this prohibition.
she was presumed a married woman. By witnesses, or she was known and recognized as a married woman (see Yad Peshutah).
but she disqualified herself from the priesthood forever. For a person is believed to forbid himself by his own admission (see below, halacha 3, and Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 18:9 and elsewhere).

and she performs chalitzah but not yibbum. She performs chalitzah in case she is a widow obligated in chalitzah, but we are stringent according to her words to forbid her to yibbum, like a divorcee, to whom the prohibition of a brother's wife applies.
even though it is not confirmed. Although the court did not validate the witnesses' signatures.
as we have explained. Above 7:1, 24. 3. But if the husband said it was conditional, etc. In these cases the get's presence with the woman is not proof that a divorce took effect.
as we have explained. Above, halacha 1.
even though she was presumed to be his wife. Although she was known as his wife, and we do not know this from her own words.
she is believed, for a woman does not brazenly lie in front of her husband. She does not have the audacity to lie and say that he divorced her, and if she claims so, she was certainly divorced.
lest he intend to ruin her. We are concerned that the husband wants to cause her a mishap, that she marry another man in violation and her children from him be mamzerim (see above 10:7).
because he believes her. When he admits that he divorced her, and so she is not afraid to lie.
even if the husband is standing, etc.. That she makes the claim in front of her husband (as above, halacha 4).
because of the witnesses who support her, she might be brazen. For it is possible that she brazenly lies in such a situation, because of the witnesses' support of her statement.
from several days ago. Long ago.
and her husband. The second, the witness.
and it is a presumption that they do not ruin themselves. We assume that they would not bring upon themselves the ruin of a prohibition and mamzerut.
since the matter is doubtful to him. To her new husband, who does not know which pair of witnesses is lying.
if they all dwelt in one courtyard. All living together in the same place, and we assume that what happens there is known to all.
for people tend to divorce discreetly. And it is possible that therefore the witnesses did not see the act of divorce, though they were in the same courtyard (and see Hilchot Ishut 9:30).
both testify that she is a married woman, etc.. Although their testimonies about the woman's current status do not match, both agree that she was a married woman.

and each of them testified for himself. That she was betrothed to him; and since their statements completely contradict one another, there is no testimony at all that she is a married woman (Rabbi Y. Kafih).

an agent for receiving. An agent appointed by the woman to receive her get on her behalf, and from the moment the get reaches his hand she is divorced as if it had been given to her herself (above 6:1).
as we have explained. Above, halacha 3.
the agent is believed. Because handing the get to him is a declaration by the husband that he relies on him and agrees to whatever he does with it (Bavli Gittin 64a).

she is doubtfully divorced, for she was presumed to be a married woman, etc.. . We leave her in her presumptive status, but we are also concerned that the agent carried out his mission and divorced her (see Hilchot Terumot 4:6).
as we have explained. Above, halacha 11, that the agent is believed to say he received the get for divorce, and here witnesses testify that they received it.
and there is peace between him and her, and peace in the world. These situations will be explained below (13:1-3); only then is she believed to testify to his death.

it is a presumption that she does not ruin herself... in a matter that is bound to be revealed to all, etc.. She certainly would not risk a false matter that will be revealed without any possibility of denying it or arguing against it.

and she would forbid herself to this one and that one... and bring forth her children as mamzerim. She would be forbidden to the first and second husbands, and her children from both would be mamzerim (as explained above 10:5, 7, regarding one who married two men by mistake).
and a witness from the mouth of a witness, etc.. That the witness heard from another person; such testimony is not accepted in other testimonies (ibid. 17:1-5).
from the mouths of relatives. Their family members, who are disqualified from testifying in other testimonies (ibid. chapter 13).
from five women. Above 7:3.
a gentile speaking casually. Where the information about the husband's death was said in the course of his conversation, without intending to testify.
as will be explained. Below 13:11.
but if he intended to testify, he is not believed. For a gentile is disqualified from testifying (Hilchot Edut 9:4).
one disqualified by a Torah transgression. Disqualified from testifying because he committed a Torah transgression (Hilchot Edut 10:1-4).
disqualified by rabbinic law. Because he committed a transgression of rabbinic law (ibid.).

she does not leave her permission... and the words of one are not in place of two. The witness who said that the husband died and permitted her through him is considered as two witnesses, so one witness lacks the power to contradict him.
both came together. Two witnesses who contradict one another came and testified together.

and she says: It is clear to me that he died, she does not leave. That it is clear to her that he died. And she does not leave because neither she nor the witness herself has any doubt (as above, halacha 7).
where the one on whose word she married was like the two who came and contradicted him. . of equal standing in qualification to testify.
it is like half and half. The weight of their testimony is equal, as in the previous halacha.

for we do not say two are like a hundred except with valid witnesses. The power of two witnesses equals the power of a hundred, and the majority does not decide, leaving the doubt evenly balanced (Hilchot Edut 18:3). This rule applies only to valid witnesses, not to those who were disqualified from testimony and then made eligible.
and if she married one of her witnesses, etc.. For neither of them has any doubt that the husband died (as above, halacha 7).
she may marry on her own word. She is permitted to marry on the basis of her own testimony.
as we have informed. Above, halacha 15.
and her co-wife is forbidden. The other wife of the same husband.

and even if this one married first, we do not say, etc.. Even if the one who said "my husband died" married another because of her statement, we do not rely on her testimony to permit her co-wife, since we are concerned that she is trying to prove her statement correct in order to ruin her co-wife when it becomes known that the husband is still alive, even if she herself would be forbidden to her second husband.
she may marry in accordance with, etc.. The one who testified that he died; and we do not treat the co-wife's testimony as forbidding her.
was killed. Died an unnatural death.
since both say he is not alive, they may marry. Although their testimonies contradict one another, both testify that he is not alive.
and peace in the world. There is no war (as below, halacha 2).

for this one is presumed a liar and wants to escape from under her husband. For at first she claimed before her husband that he divorced her, and this claim suffices to permit her (see Hilchot Ishut 16:26), and from the witnesses' words it was proven that she is prone to lying in order to be permitted, and therefore she is not believed in testimony about the husband's death either.
she may not marry, lest she hired him. Just as she was presumed to lie, so she is suspected of causing the witness to lie.
for she has a witness. For one can rely on one witness in testimony of death (above 12:15).
peace between her and him. That there was no dispute between them (as above, halacha 1).

lest she base her opinion on matters most of which result in death. We are concerned that she bases her words on events from which most people die, that her husband was there, and she assumes he died.
that the first and the last were killed. The people before him and after him.

she is not believed, even if she said: He died in the war and I buried him. Because it is possible that in the tumult of war she did not identify with certainty, and perhaps buried another person, and the like (compare below, halacha 5).
but if she said: He died on his bed. That his death was not connected to the war.

she may not marry initially, but if she married, she does not leave. For it was not decided whether she is believed in all her words, since she was careful to say that there was a war though there was no need, or whether, since there was a war, she does not know that he died for certain but is estimating.
my husband died under the collapse. He was killed when the house fell on him and on others.
and likewise if there was an outbreak of snakes and scorpions. A strike of venomous snakes and scorpions.
they set a house on fire around us. They lit a fire at the entrance of the place where we were hiding, and it filled with smoke.
just as a miracle was done for her, etc.. The fact that she survived proves that the case did not involve certain death.
it was a year of famine... she is not believed. Lest she assume her husband died because many died of hunger.
he died and I buried him. In such a case there is no concern that she spoke out of assumption.
fell upon. Attacked.
bandits. Robbers.
for it is not their way to kill women, so that it be said, etc.. Since they generally do not harm women, her survival is no proof that the husband too could have survived.
there was a plague in the world. Death from an epidemic of disease.
for it is a matter commonly known to everyone. Clear and known to all.
we are not concerned that she relied on the majority of the dead. Rather she saw with certainty that her husband too died.
we have already said. Above 12:15.
he heard from the children. He heard children talking.
so many mourners were there, and so-and-so the sage, etc.. From their speech it is evident that this was a real event and not a children's game.

for a person does not declare himself wicked. A person is not made guilty by his own testimony, so although he admitted to murder he is not disqualified from testifying, and his testimony about the deceased is accepted (Hilchot Edut 3:7; 12:2).
we have already said. Above 12:17.
an excuse. Another reason.

this is not one speaking casually, for his intention is to frighten this person. In such a case he is not considered one speaking casually about the death of that person, because there is another reason for his saying that he died: to frighten the person before him.
they strengthen themselves with falsehood etc.. They boast of their strength, even if it is not true.
he is believed. Even though they asked and questioned him, he did not leave the category of one speaking casually.
we have already informed. Above 12:15.
who stands and sees all around him. So that the whole of it can be seen at one glance.
and stayed long enough for his soul to depart. He remained in the water for a time sufficient to cause death.
a net. A fishing net.
a limb that cannot be removed from a living person without his dying. A limb whose severing certainly causes death.
a fiery furnace. A large oven.
a cauldron. A large pot.
its two signs. The windpipe and the gullet, whose severing certainly causes death.
crucified. Hanged.
he does not testify about him. That he died, since perhaps he was saved.

and if she married, she need not leave. Because the witness has no personal stake in the matter, unlike the woman, and therefore the concern that his testimony was inaccurate is smaller (compare above, halacha 2).
in water that has no end. Such as a sea (see above, halacha 16).
and his memory was lost and his name forgotten. That nothing was heard from him again, and it seems that he did not come up elsewhere either.
as we have explained. Above, halacha 16.
they excommunicate him. Because he ruled contrary to halacha.
they found him slain or dead. His identity must be verified in order to testify about his death.
his forehead. His brow.
and in his clothes. In his garments.
even a mole. A kind of small wart, whose presence in a particular place on a person's body is a sign of identity.
because the features of his face change. And it is possible to err in identifying him.
hours. Several hours.
and it has swollen. The body has begun to swell.
even at night. And we are not concerned that the darkness would prevent a correct identification.
and the messenger does not know who he is. He does not know the dead man, but knows only his name.
even though the gentile does not know that man. That he is not acquainted with that man.
provided that he says: I buried him. For then it is clear that the man is dead, and he is not speaking by estimate (Yad Peshutah).
bound in a collar. Captives or prisoners bound in iron chains.
his appearance was thus and thus, and his signs were thus and thus. But he does not know his name and identity.
Jewish handwriting. Written by a Jew.
one who became mute. Unable to speak.
and they examine him the way they examine for divorce documents. To make sure he is of sound mind and has not gone insane (see above 2:16).

and they do not examine the witnesses of a woman by inquiry and cross-examination. Witnesses who come to permit a woman out of her state of being an agunah (a woman unable to remarry) are not examined meticulously about details of place and time, unlike ordinary testimony (Hilchot Edut 1:4-5).
for the Sages did not say a matter etc.. The purpose of the leniency is to allow the woman to marry another, so that she will not be forbidden all her life.
the severe forbidden union. A married woman, who is forbidden by a severe prohibition.
as we have explained. Above 12:15 ff.

in a matter that you can only establish from the mouths of witnesses and through their testimony. Valid witnesses are required only when knowledge of the truth rests on the witnesses' words alone and there is no way to verify the matter by other means.
and the witness cannot evade if the matter is not true. For if the man about whom they testified that he died comes, the witness will not be able to justify his words, but will be caught in his lie.
